RT @uwu_underground: Emo time, chat.

Just wanna shout out this entire community.

If you told me years ago we'd be doing a live show with @dustrial at @defcon, I would've called absolute bullshit and asked what you were trying to sell me.

But here we are.

We love this community more than we know how to say without becoming embarrassingly sincere on main. Every time one of you messages us saying you learned about an APT, spotted a scam, discovered some cursed corner of infosec history, or decided to start learning because of something we made, it means everything.

This project can be brutally hard sometimes.

Today, the girls showed me a collection of screenshots from people who learned something, bettered themselves, found support, or poured their hearts out over our work, image, or message.

I cried like a fucking child. These tears are still running down my face while I am typing this right now.

So, genuinely, thank you.

As long as we keep this project alive, we will keep educating, supporting people, calling out scams, bullying snake oil merchants, and doing everything we can to inspire this community to learn, grow, and become better than the industry expected you to be. 

We want to work with more places in the community to achieve this in the future so very much 

We love you mammals. 
☯️

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: This kernel rootkit takes its C2 commands through the Windows registry.

It registers a CmRegisterCallbackEx routine, then the user-mode agent writes commands into a benign key using nothing but standard registry APIs. Every write gets checked for the magic value 0x2625B7146B and the command is unpacked from it.

No IOCTL. No DeviceIoControl. No named pipe. Nothing on the user-mode side that looks like it is talking to a driver at all.

The command set behind it is a full kernel toolkit: arbitrary physical memory read and write by building a custom page table and injecting it into a free PML4 slot, PFN database reads, KVA shadow bypass, kernel APC DLL injection, ETW and CKCL and syscall table hooks, HvlGetQpcBias and GetCpuClock patched for timing.

Then the HWID spoofing shows up. Disk, Nvidia GPU, SMBIOS, plus forged mouhid and i8042prt input packets.

This started life as a game cheat driver. The cheat scene has been shipping production grade kernel capability for a decade and it keeps getting laundered into malware.

Author: @xeroxsec 

Full analysis, IOCs and a YARA rule by 0xSec:
https://t.co/T4GX6pKFqN

The C2 infrastructure was still live and unflagged on VirusTotal at time of writing.

- Allocate and write a return stub
- Locate SMA.dll

- Scan for a pointer to AmsiScanBuffer
- Overwrite the pointer with the stub address https://t.co/iWqoEIlSDh
